body:
What is a national Emergency?

A national Emergency is an extraordinary constitutional arrangement under Article 352. It permits the Union government to exercise additional powers when specified threats endanger the security of India or part of its territory.

The constitutional grounds have changed over time. In 1975, Article 352 permitted an Emergency on the ground of internal disturbance. That expression was later replaced by armed rebellion through the 44th Constitutional Amendment.

The proclamation of 25 June 1975

On 25 June 1975, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi recommended a national Emergency to President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed. The President issued a proclamation under Article 352 on the ground that internal disturbances threatened India's security.

Major opposition leaders were arrested during the night of 25–26 June. The Union Cabinet was informed at a meeting on the morning of 26 June, after the proclamation had already been issued. The events exposed weaknesses in the constitutional safeguards then applicable to Emergency proclamations.

The Emergency proclaimed in June 1975 continued until 21 March 1977.

How did the Emergency affect government?

Under an Article 352 Emergency, the Union government acquires extraordinary authority. Article 353 extends Union executive powers to directions concerning how States exercise their executive authority. Parliament also acquires power under Article 250 to legislate on matters normally included in the State List.

This produces greater centralisation of government power. However, it does not mean that all State governments are automatically dismissed. That is a separate issue from President's Rule under Article 356.

Restrictions on civil liberties

Civil liberties include protections that allow individuals to express opinions, associate with others, oppose government policies and seek legal remedies against unlawful State action.

During the Emergency, several restrictions were imposed:

  • Press censorship: Newspapers were required to obtain prior approval before publishing certain material. Critical reporting was restricted.
  • Preventive detention: Opposition leaders, political workers and other individuals were detained without the normal procedure of a criminal trial.
  • Restrictions on protest: Political demonstrations, strikes and other forms of public mobilisation were prohibited or severely restricted.
  • Limits on legal remedies: Presidential orders restricted access to courts for enforcing specified Fundamental Rights.
  • Administrative excesses: Forced sterilisation, coercive population-control practices and demolitions or displacement of poor settlements occurred in several places.

Preventive detention and habeas corpus

Preventive detention permits detention to prevent a feared future act rather than as punishment following conviction for a completed offence. Such detention raises significant questions about individual liberty and the availability of legal safeguards.

Habeas corpus is a judicial remedy through which a court examines whether a person's detention is lawful and can order release if the detention is unlawful.

During the Emergency, the Maintenance of Internal Security Act, 1971 (MISA) was extensively used for preventive detention. The government argued that the relevant Emergency orders prevented courts from entertaining petitions challenging many detentions.

The Supreme Court's habeas corpus decision

In ADM Jabalpur v. Shivakant Shukla (1976), commonly called the Habeas Corpus case, a majority of the Supreme Court accepted severe restrictions on judicial challenges to detention during the Emergency.

Justice H. R. Khanna dissented. He argued against treating personal liberty as entirely dependent on the availability of a particular constitutional remedy. The majority decision is widely regarded as a serious failure to protect civil liberties; its reasoning was rejected by the Supreme Court in Justice K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017).

The constitutional distinction: Articles 358 and 359

It is inaccurate to say that a national Emergency automatically abolishes every Fundamental Right.

At the time of the 1975 Emergency, Article 358 affected the protection of freedoms under Article 19, while Presidential orders under Article 359 restricted the right to approach courts for enforcement of specified other Fundamental Rights. The legal effect depended on the constitutional provisions and orders then in force.

The later 44th Amendment introduced important protections, including preventing the suspension of access to courts for enforcement of Articles 20 and 21. Those present safeguards should not be incorrectly projected backwards onto the legal arrangements operating in 1975.

The 42nd Constitutional Amendment of 1976

During the Emergency, Parliament enacted the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976. Among its major changes were:

  • Adding Socialist and Secular to the Preamble.
  • Changing the Preamble's expression concerning national unity to include Integrity.
  • Adding Fundamental Duties through Article 51A.
  • Extending the ordinary term of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies from 5 years to 6 years.

The 44th Amendment later restored the ordinary legislative term to 5 years.

Prelims focus

  • The 1975 Emergency was proclaimed on 25 June 1975 under Article 352.
  • The President who issued the proclamation was Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed.
  • The ground used in 1975 was internal disturbance.
  • MISA was used for preventive detention.
  • ADM Jabalpur v. Shivakant Shukla was decided in 1976; Justice H. R. Khanna dissented.
  • Trap: Article 352 concerns national Emergency; Article 356 concerns failure of constitutional government in a State.

[NCERT, Class 12, Politics in India Since Independence, chapter 6, The Crisis of Democratic Order, printed pp. 108–117; Ministry of Home Affairs, Gazette of India, Emergency proclamation dated 25 June 1975; Supreme Court of India, ADM Jabalpur v. Shivakant Shukla, judgment dated 28 April 1976; Ministry of Law and Justice, Constitution of India, Articles 250, 352, 353, 358 and 359, edition as on 10 September 2026. Consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The 1975 Emergency expanded Union authority while restricting political participation and access to judicial remedies.
pictures.caption: How Emergency powers affected democratic institutions and individual rights.

title: The National Emergency of 1975–1977: Proclamation, Restrictions and Civil Liberties

body:
The decision to hold elections

In January 1977, the government announced Lok Sabha elections. Opposition leaders began returning to political activity after their detention during the Emergency.

Several opposition groups joined together to form the Janata Party. Leaders associated with the movement against the Emergency, including Jayaprakash Narayan, helped unite these forces. The campaign emphasised civil liberties, democratic government and opposition to the abuses committed during the Emergency.

The Lok Sabha election of March 1977

The 1977 Lok Sabha election resulted in the defeat of Congress and the formation of the first non-Congress government at the Centre. Morarji Desai became Prime Minister on 24 March 1977.

This was a major event in Indian democracy because voters removed a powerful ruling party through elections, and power was transferred to its political opponents.

The political verdict was particularly strong against Congress in much of northern India. Electoral behaviour was not identical across all regions; Congress retained substantial support in parts of southern India.

When did the Emergency end?

The national Emergency proclaimed on 25 June 1975 was formally revoked on 21 March 1977. The revocation proclamation was issued by B. D. Jatti, the Vice-President then acting as President.

Therefore, the President associated with the original Emergency proclamation and the person who formally revoked it were different.

The Shah Commission of Inquiry

In May 1977, the Janata government appointed the Shah Commission of Inquiry, headed by retired Chief Justice J. C. Shah.

The Commission investigated allegations of abuse of authority during the Emergency. Its inquiries covered preventive detention, censorship, coercive sterilisation, forced displacement and the misuse of administrative powers.

The Commission's investigations demonstrated why accountability matters when extraordinary powers are exercised.

The 44th Constitutional Amendment of 1978

The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 introduced safeguards designed to reduce the possibility of misuse of national Emergency provisions.

Grounds for proclaiming an Emergency

Under Article 352, a national Emergency may now be proclaimed when India's security, or the security of part of its territory, is threatened by:

  • War;
  • External aggression; or
  • Armed rebellion.

The expression internal disturbance, used in 1975, is no longer an independent ground for proclaiming an Emergency under Article 352.

Written decision and parliamentary approval

The President may issue a national Emergency proclamation only after the decision of the Union Cabinet has been communicated to the President in writing. The Union Cabinet here means the Prime Minister and ministers of Cabinet rank.

Ordinarily, the proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within 1 month. Each House must pass the approval resolution by:

  • A majority of its total membership; and
  • At least two-thirds of the members present and voting.

Both conditions must be satisfied in each House. Once approved, the proclamation may continue, unless revoked earlier, for 6 months from the date on which the second House passes its approval resolution. Further continuation requires renewed approval by both Houses for successive periods of 6 months. Special provisions apply when the Lok Sabha is dissolved: Rajya Sabha approval can preserve the proclamation temporarily, but the reconstituted Lok Sabha must approve it within 30 days of its first sitting.

The President can revoke the proclamation. If the Lok Sabha passes a resolution disapproving it by a simple majority of members present and voting, the President must revoke it.

Protection of Fundamental Rights

The current constitutional provisions also distinguish between 2 different effects:

ProvisionCurrent rule
Article 358Article 19 automatically ceases to restrict the State's legislative and executive powers only during an Emergency based on war or external aggression. This protection covers only laws expressly declaring their relation to the Emergency and executive action under such laws.
Article 359The President may suspend the right to move courts for enforcement of specified Fundamental Rights, but not Articles 20 and 21.
Article 20Provides protections concerning conviction and punishment for offences.
Article 21Protects life and personal liberty.

Article 359 concerns the enforcement of specified rights through courts. It should not be described as an automatic disappearance of all constitutional rights.

Political developments after 1977

The Janata Party included leaders from several political traditions and experienced internal disputes. Its government lost power in 1979. A short-lived government headed by Charan Singh followed.

In the 1980 Lok Sabha election, Congress under Indira Gandhi returned to power, winning 353 seats. The result showed that the defeat of a party in one election did not prevent its democratic return through a later election.

A further change occurred after the 1989 Lok Sabha election. No single party obtained a majority, and a long period of coalition and minority governments began. Regional parties became increasingly important in forming or supporting national governments.

The constitutional rules explained here reflect the official Constitution of India as on 10 September 2026. They must be distinguished from the less restrictive legal framework under which the 1975 Emergency was proclaimed.

Prelims focus

  • The Emergency was revoked on 21 March 1977 by B. D. Jatti, acting as President.
  • Morarji Desai headed the first non-Congress Union government in 1977.
  • The Shah Commission was appointed in May 1977 under J. C. Shah.
  • The 44th Amendment replaced internal disturbance with armed rebellion.
  • National Emergency approval ordinarily requires a special majority in both Houses within 1 month.
  • Trap: Article 358 and Article 359 do not operate in the same manner.

[NCERT, Class 12, Politics in India Since Independence, chapter 6, The Crisis of Democratic Order, printed pp. 113–124; NCERT, Politics in India Since Independence, Recent Developments in Indian Politics, section Era of Coalitions; Ministry of Home Affairs, Gazette of India, revocation proclamation dated 21 March 1977; Ministry of Law and Justice, Constitution of India, Articles 352, 358 and 359, edition as on 10 September 2026. Historical sources and constitutional text consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Democratic restoration and constitutional reform after the Emergency.

title: The Restoration of Democracy in 1977 and Safeguards Against Future Emergencies

body:
Why did popular movements become important?

Elections are an important means of political participation, but they are not the only way citizens express demands. A popular movement brings people together around shared grievances, interests or goals and seeks changes in public policy or social conditions.

During the 1970s and 1980s, many social groups felt that political parties were not adequately addressing their problems. Farmers, landless labourers, Dalits, women and other groups organised collective action to make their demands visible.

Party-based and non-party movements

Some movements were linked to political parties, trade unions or ideological organisations. Others operated independently of political parties. These were sometimes described as non-party political formations.

The word political does not necessarily mean contesting elections. A movement can influence government decisions by organising public meetings, rallies, petitions, negotiations, demonstrations and other forms of collective action.

Farmers' movements: different groups, different concerns

Indian agriculture includes landowners, small cultivators, tenant farmers, sharecroppers and agricultural labourers. Their interests may overlap, but they are not always identical.

A landless agricultural worker may primarily demand land rights or higher wages. A farmer who sells crops in the market may be more concerned with crop prices, electricity charges, irrigation and loan repayment.

Naxalbari and land-based agrarian protest

In 1967, a peasant uprising occurred in Naxalbari, in the Darjeeling region of West Bengal. Its background included disputes concerning landownership, tenancy and exploitation of cultivators.

The movement became associated with radical communist politics and the advocacy of armed revolution. In 1969, the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) emerged under the leadership of Charu Majumdar.

For examination purposes, Naxalbari should be distinguished from later farmers' organisations that primarily used mass demonstrations and political bargaining to seek better agricultural prices and facilities.

Bharatiya Kisan Union

The Bharatiya Kisan Union (BKU) became an influential organisation in the farmers' movements of the 1980s, particularly in western Uttar Pradesh and neighbouring areas of Haryana.

Mahendra Singh Tikait was a prominent leader associated with the movement. Many participants were farmers who produced crops for sale in markets and had benefited from agricultural changes during the Green Revolution period.

The BKU raised demands such as:

  • Higher or more favourable government procurement and support prices for agricultural produce.
  • Affordable and reliable electricity for agriculture.
  • Relief from agricultural debt.
  • Fewer restrictions on the movement and sale of farm produce.
  • Improved economic security for farmers.

In January 1988, thousands of BKU farmers gathered in Meerut, Uttar Pradesh, to protest against increased electricity charges. Their prolonged demonstration became a prominent example of organised rural political pressure.

Other farmers' organisations

Shetkari Sanghatana emerged as an important farmers' organisation in Maharashtra. It argued that agricultural producers were disadvantaged by economic policies favouring urban and industrial sectors.

The Bharatiya Kisan Union and Shetkari Sanghatana both represented important aspects of agrarian mobilisation, but their political networks and regional bases differed.

Dalit assertion after Independence

The Constitution established equality before the law and prohibited caste-based untouchability. Article 17 abolished untouchability and forbade its practice in any form.

However, legal abolition did not immediately end discrimination, social exclusion, economic inequality or violence against Dalits. Movements emerged to demand effective implementation of equality and social justice.

The Dalit Panthers

The Dalit Panthers were founded in Maharashtra in 1972 by young Dalit activists. The organisation drew inspiration from the ideas of Dr. B. R. Ambedkar and challenged continued caste oppression after Independence.

Its major concerns included:

  • Violence and atrocities against Dalits.
  • Denial of equality, dignity and access to common resources.
  • Economic exploitation and social exclusion.
  • Effective implementation of reservations and other social-justice measures.

Dalit literature, poetry and autobiographical writing also became important forms of protest and public expression. Writers described lived experiences of discrimination and challenged the social assumptions supporting caste inequality.

The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 later strengthened the legal framework against specified caste-based atrocities. Its enactment formed part of a broader history of Dalit assertion and demands for legal protection; it should not be attributed to any single organisation alone.

How farmers' and Dalit movements differed

Farmers' organisations such as the BKU primarily sought changes in agricultural prices and economic policy. Dalit Panthers placed caste discrimination, social dignity and protection from atrocities at the centre of their mobilisation. Landless agrarian movements raised different issues again, particularly access to land and protection from exploitation.

Prelims focus

  • Naxalbari uprising: 1967, West Bengal.
  • Charu Majumdar was associated with the CPI (Marxist-Leninist), formed in 1969.
  • BKU became prominent in the 1980s; its Meerut agitation occurred in 1988.
  • Dalit Panthers were formed in Maharashtra in 1972.
  • Article 17 abolishes untouchability.
  • Trap: The main demands of market-oriented farmers' organisations were not identical to those of landless agricultural workers.

[NCERT, Class 12, Politics in India Since Independence, chapter 6, The Crisis of Democratic Order, printed pp. 104–105; chapter 7, Rise of Popular Movements, printed pp. 129–135; Ministry of Law and Justice, Constitution of India, Article 17, edition as on 10 September 2026; India Code, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. Consulted 23 November 2026.]

title: Popular Movements, Farmers' Demands and Dalit Assertion
